editorSelection.selectedText:
The whole structure rests on one invariant, and it is worth saying out loud before writing the code:

> **`tree[i]` is the correct summary of node `i`'s range, assuming the tags sitting on `i`'s ancestors have not yet been applied to it.**

Equivalently, `tree[i]` already accounts for `i`'s own tag and everything below it, but is behind on whatever is still pending above. The tree is never storing wrong data; it is storing data with a known debt, and **the debt always lives above you**. The true value of a leaf is its stored value transformed by every tag on the root-to-leaf path.

Each operation then checks out against that invariant directly.

`apply` transforms a node's summary and merges the tag into that node's own tag. The node is now correct including the new operation, and its descendants are behind by one more tag, which the invariant permits.

`push` moves a tag down one level, transforming both children's summaries and merging the tag into theirs before clearing its own. It deliberately does **not** touch `tree[i]`, which is correct because `tree[i]` already included that tag. Pushing does not change what the tree means; it only relocates the debt downwards.

Stopping on full containment is legitimate precisely because the invariant never claimed the descendants were up to date. You are allowed to leave.

Pushing **before** recursing on a partial overlap is the step that matters most. After the push, the children carry no hidden debt from their parent, so they can be modified as though this were an ordinary tree. Skip it, and you will modify a child and then later push a stale tag down on top of your modification, which is exactly the classic lazy bug.

Recombining on the way back up restores the parent after its children changed. Omit it and the parent lies silently from then on.

The query may return `tree[i]` on containment only because it pushed at every node on the way down, so all the debt above `i` has already been settled onto it.
